asn.name: ASN
asn.def: A number that identifies one network on the internet that is run by a single organisation and has its own routing policy, for example AS13335 for Cloudflare. ASNs are how networks are named in BGP.

bgp.name: BGP
bgp.def: The protocol networks use to tell each other which IP address ranges they can reach. Your traffic follows the paths BGP has learned, so a wrong or missing BGP announcement can make a network unreachable.

prefix.name: Prefix
prefix.def: A block of IP addresses written as an address plus a length, such as 203.0.113.0/24. In BGP, networks announce prefixes to say which addresses they own or carry.

cidr.name: CIDR
cidr.def: The notation for an address range as an address plus the number of leading network bits, for example 10.0.0.0/22. A larger number after the slash means a smaller range.

rpki.name: RPKI
rpki.def: A signed registry that lets an address owner state which AS may announce their prefixes. Routers can use it to drop announcements that do not match, which helps stop route hijacks and mistakes.

roa.name: ROA
roa.def: A signed RPKI record saying that a given AS is allowed to announce a given prefix up to a given length. A route with no matching ROA is 'not found'; one that contradicts a ROA is 'invalid'.

irr.name: IRR
irr.def: A set of public databases where networks record their routing policy and route objects. Many providers build their BGP filters from IRR data, so a missing entry can stop your prefix from being accepted.

ix.name: IX
ix.def: A shared switching point where many networks connect directly to each other to swap traffic, usually giving shorter paths and lower latency than going through a transit provider.

peeringdb.name: PeeringDB
peeringdb.def: A community-maintained database where networks publish who they are, where they connect and how they like to peer. It is the usual place to find a network's exchange points and contacts.

hop.name: Traceroute hop
hop.def: One router on the path between you and the target. Traceroute lists each hop in order, with the time it took to get a reply from it.

rtt.name: RTT
rtt.def: How long a packet takes to reach a target and for the reply to come back, in milliseconds. Distance, routing and congestion all add to it.

packet-loss.name: Packet loss
packet-loss.def: The share of test packets that got no reply. A little loss on one router in the middle of a path is often harmless (it may just rate-limit replies); loss that continues to the target is a real problem.

ttl-dns.name: TTL (DNS)
ttl-dns.def: How many seconds a resolver may keep a DNS answer in its cache before asking again. A low TTL makes changes show up faster; a high one reduces lookups.

ttl-ip.name: TTL (IP)
ttl-ip.def: A counter in every IP packet that drops by one at each router. When it reaches zero the router discards the packet and sends back an error. Traceroute uses this to discover each hop.

ptr.name: PTR
ptr.def: A DNS record that maps an IP address back to a hostname (the reverse of an A or AAAA record). Mail servers often check it to decide whether a sender looks legitimate.

fcrdns.name: FCrDNS
fcrdns.def: A check that the hostname in an IP's PTR record resolves back to that same IP. Passing it shows the owner controls both the reverse and the forward DNS.

a.name: A record
a.def: A DNS record that maps a hostname to an IPv4 address.

aaaa.name: AAAA record
aaaa.def: A DNS record that maps a hostname to an IPv6 address.

cname.name: CNAME
cname.def: A DNS record that makes one name an alias of another. Resolvers follow it and use the target's records. A name with a CNAME cannot hold other record types.

mx.name: MX
mx.def: A DNS record that says which servers accept email for a domain. Each has a priority number; senders try the lowest number first.

ns.name: NS
ns.def: A DNS record that lists the servers that are authoritative for a domain, meaning the ones that hold the real answers.

soa.name: SOA
soa.def: A DNS record at the top of a zone with its primary name server, the admin contact, a serial number that rises with each change and timers for secondary servers.

txt.name: TXT
txt.def: A DNS record that holds free text. It is used for SPF, DKIM, DMARC and for proving you own a domain to a service.

caa.name: CAA
caa.def: A DNS record that lists which certificate authorities may issue certificates for your domain. Authorities must check it before issuing.

dnssec.name: DNSSEC
dnssec.def: A set of signatures that lets a resolver check that a DNS answer really came from the zone owner and was not altered on the way.

spf.name: SPF
spf.def: A DNS TXT record that lists the servers allowed to send email for your domain. Receivers use it to spot forged senders. It may cause at most 10 DNS lookups.

dkim.name: DKIM
dkim.def: A digital signature added to outgoing email. The receiver looks up your public key in DNS to check that the message was sent by your domain and was not changed.

dkim-selector.name: DKIM selector
dkim-selector.def: A label that says which DKIM key signed a message. The public key lives at selector._domainkey.yourdomain, so one domain can use several keys at once.

dmarc.name: DMARC
dmarc.full: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance
dmarc.def: A DNS record that tells receivers what to do with mail that fails SPF and DKIM checks for your domain (nothing, quarantine or reject) and where to send reports.

bimi.name: BIMI
bimi.def: A DNS record that points to your logo so supporting mailbox providers can show it next to your messages. It normally needs an enforced DMARC policy first.

mta-sts.name: MTA-STS
mta-sts.def: A policy, published in DNS and over HTTPS, that tells other mail servers to deliver to you only over a verified TLS connection.

tls-rpt.name: TLS-RPT
tls-rpt.def: A DNS record that asks other mail servers to send you daily reports about TLS problems when delivering to your domain.

dnsbl.name: DNSBL
dnsbl.def: A public list of IP addresses or domains seen sending spam or abuse, queried through DNS. Mail servers use these lists to reject or flag mail.

rdap.name: RDAP
rdap.def: The modern, structured replacement for WHOIS. It answers over HTTPS in JSON and is served by registries and by the regional internet registries for IP ranges.

whois.name: WHOIS
whois.def: The long-standing protocol for looking up who registered a domain or holds an IP range. Most registries now redact personal details.

registrar.name: Registrar
registrar.def: The company you buy and renew a domain through. It passes your registration to the registry that runs the domain ending (.com, .in and so on).

epp-status.name: EPP status
epp-status.def: Flags on a domain that show its state and locks, for example clientTransferProhibited (the registrar has locked it against transfers) or pendingDelete (it is being removed).

ttfb.name: TTFB
ttfb.def: How long after sending a request you wait for the first byte of the reply. It includes the server's processing time, so slow code, no caching or a distant server all raise it.

tls-handshake.name: TLS handshake
tls-handshake.def: The exchange at the start of an HTTPS connection where both sides agree on encryption and the server proves its identity. It costs one or two network round trips.

cert-chain.name: Certificate chain
cert-chain.def: The series of certificates from your site's certificate, through one or more intermediates, up to a root that browsers already trust. If a link is missing, some clients show an error.

san.name: SAN
san.def: The list of hostnames a certificate is valid for. A browser accepts the certificate only if the name in the address bar is on this list.

port-open.name: Open port
port-open.def: Something is listening on the port and accepted the connection.

port-closed.name: Closed port
port-closed.def: The machine answered, but nothing is listening on that port.

port-filtered.name: Filtered port
port-filtered.def: There was no answer at all, which usually means a firewall is silently dropping the traffic.
